1:
The wish is put as a question in the Hebrew, and three of the commentators say so. Gill gives the ancient versions their literal who will give to my head water; Ellicott notes that in Hebrew as in Latin a question was the natural way to utter a desire; Calvin says simply that the phrase means a wish. They agree also on where the verse belongs. In the Hebrew manuscripts it stands as the last of the preceding chapter, and Clarke and Calvin both think it belongs there. Ellicott alone refuses to settle it that way: the verse is closely tied to what precedes and even more closely to what follows, so that strictly there ought to be no break at all and the discourse should run on.

What the grief is for they take differently. Gill has the head dissolved into water and the eyes running as from a spring, and adds that even this would not suffice. Henry finds the same Hebrew word serving for the eye and for a fountain, as if in this vale of tears our eyes were meant for weeping rather than seeing. Ellicott corrects the figure slightly, the word being a tank or reservoir rather than a spring. Calvin explains why the prophet reaches for such comparisons: he took no delight in them and was not embellishing his discourse, but seeing their hearts inflexible and plain speech despised, he was constrained to it. Clarke hears in the verse the language of many a pastor who has preached long to a hardened people to little effect.

On the lodging place they converge. Keil and Delitzsch insist it is not a resting place under the open sky but a harbour for travellers, a building put up on the caravan route. Ellicott names it a khan or caravanserai and recalls the shelter a son of Barzillai raised near Bethlehem in munificent gratitude to his adopted country. Clarke says the east has no inns such as Europe knows, only public buildings without furniture or food, often without a roof, mere walls against the wild beasts of the desert. Calvin distinguishes them from the inns of towns, calling them sheds thrown up along a long road for a traveller overtaken by the dark. Wesley reduces it to a mean hut.

Clarke raises a question the others do not: whether the wish is the prophet's at all. Several interpreters, he reports, suppose the verse to be the speech of God; he cannot receive it, holding that the prophet speaks here and God takes up the discourse only with the next verse. Henry guards the wish from being taken as a plan. The prophet had work among them which he must not quit for his own ease; we are not to go out of the world, bad as it is, before our time, and if he could not reform them he could bear a testimony against them. Calvin thinks the wish inflamed the people, and finds that necessary: since a man's native soil is naturally dear, the desire to leave measures how far they had gone.

The two words of accusation are then weighed. Calvin takes adulterers metaphorically, of all who had departed from God and were immersed in every defilement rather than of the merely unchaste. Keil and Delitzsch pair adultery and faithlessness as the cardinal sins and read the second of conduct towards one's fellows here rather than towards God. Ellicott will not choose, taking them as adulterers alike spiritually and literally. On the second word Calvin gives an etymology: the noun means a summoned assembly which men are bound by oath or law to attend and may not leave, so exposing the consent and union of the people in their sins, a community holding to its wickedness as though convened for it. Gill and Henry both take the treachery as universal.
3:
The bow is a figure the translators softened, and Ellicott objects: the inserted words turn a bold metaphor into a tame simile, where the Hebrew makes the tongue itself the bow of lies. Calvin works the verb, which can mean to walk or to stretch and is often used of bows, and refuses the noun as a genitive, though his own literal rendering ends up their lying bow. Gill has much the same, their deceitful bow, and cites the Targum for it. Clarke leaves the grammar for the effect: lies take away life as fully as the keenest arrow, and here the false prophets told the people no desolation was at hand, so they made no preparation, did not return, and the sword destroyed them.

The next clause is one Ellicott is sorry to correct. They are not valiant for the truth has gained a proverbial character among champions of abstract right, and he parts with it regretfully: the Hebrew means they are not mighty for faithfulness in the land, that is, they do not rule faithfully. Calvin reaches a harsher version of the same point. They grew strong precisely because truth and equity were trodden underfoot, marching as victors once nobody dared restrain them; he notes the alternative that they had crept into their honours by fraud, and that the charge is aimed at the chief men, not the common people. Clarke puts it in a line: they are bold in sin and courageous to support their lies, but the truth they neither patronise nor support.

Whether the warning to beware one's neighbour is advice or autopsy divides them. Gill takes it as advice: do not be too credulous, keep clear of such company, since evil communications corrupt good manners. Calvin denies it outright. This is not an admonition exhorting men to be wary, he says, but a statement that no fidelity was left; it charges the people with being natural monsters, since even among the worst some regard for kindred survives. Ellicott finds the bitterness partly explained by what is known of the prophet's own household, and catches the pun: the verb gave the patriarch his name of supplanter, so every brother Israelite has become a thorough-paced Jacob and the people have forfeited the name of true Israel.

On the word for the man who goes about among them the two part again. Ellicott renders it walketh a slanderer. Calvin will not have slander here, calling it too unmeaning, and argues that the word never appears in scripture except with the verb to go: it describes one who moves about veiled, rambling for an opportunity to cheat. Its root, he adds, is the word for a merchant, and because traders so often practise crafty artifices the Hebrews applied it to any man bent on deceiving. They are nearer on the next verb. Ellicott notes it is commonly rendered mock, decides the mockery here both deludes and derides, and lets the English stand; Calvin glosses it as to mock, to trifle with, to play the fool with.

Wearying themselves to commit iniquity draws out the moralists. Clarke exclaims at the drudgery of sin and the labour a man must take to get to hell, when a tenth of it spent working with God would bring him to the gate of glory. Wesley says only that they spare no labour. Calvin illustrates it with hunting, where a man undergoes more toil than any husbandman and feels none of it, kings and courtiers so blinded by the chase that they notice neither danger nor weariness; falsehood, he concludes, requires more labour than truth. On the next verse Gill and Ellicott both take the address as God's word to the prophet about the people he lives among, Gill noting that the Targum turns it on the people instead, and Ellicott that the Greek read it as deceit upon deceit.
7:
The threatened melting is read as assay rather than destruction. Clarke calls it the furnace of affliction, put to work to see whether the dross can be purged away. Calvin builds the verse on a goldsmith: a man who brings copper for gold may pass it off until it is cast into the fire, and hypocrites likewise exhibit some brightness until they come to be really proved, so their false colours avail them nothing. Ellicott sets the melting against what precedes: the balm of Gilead had proved ineffectual and the disease required a severer remedy. Wesley alone names the instrument, the fire of the Chaldean war, which burns away the deceits they trust in so that a remnant may be purified.

The question that follows, how else he should deal with the daughter of his people, is read as deliberation. Calvin says God speaks as one taking counsel, and that by admitting them as judges he leaves them no reply, so that unless they were beyond measure stupid they could not ask to be treated otherwise. He reports that nearly all the ancient versions read wickedness where the received text has daughter, and prefers the received reading. Wesley reduces the question to a sentence, that all other means have been tried. Calvin draws from it that judgment begins at the house of God, the impiety of those who profess themselves his domestics being the less tolerable. Ellicott notes that the threat to visit has been used twice already, which gives it the emphasis of iteration.

The arrow is a matter of metallurgy as much as of archery. Gill takes the participle as drawn out, as an arrow from a quiver, notes the same word used of gold beaten into plates, and adds that the Greek makes it slaying and the Targum a sharp arrow that pierces deep. Ellicott agrees, an arrow that pierceth or slayeth, and renders the last phrase more literally as inwardly. Calvin joins the two ideas: gold is said to be drawn out when refined by repeated meltings, and arrows likewise are more piercing when sharpened. He adds an observation of his own, that the future tense here stands for a present to show habitual practice, and remarks that Welsh continually does the same.

The lament for the mountains raises a question of who is speaking. Gill reports that three versions read it as an exhortation to others to take up a weeping, and holds instead that the prophet declares what he himself will do. Ellicott finds the preposition ambiguous between upon and on account of and thinks both were meant, the prophet seeing himself on the mountains; he corrects habitations to pastures and wilderness to open country. Calvin turns the geography into an argument. The people thought themselves safe on level ground, when the plains were the most accessible; and the mountains, where a retreat is normally sought because enemies dread ambushes there, would be overrun too. Wesley puts it briefly, that the mountains could not secure them nor the valleys feed them.

Calvin also disputes a word, denying that the verb means burnt up and insisting on desolate, deserted so completely that none pass over. He closes by observing that the birds felt the judgment of God while the men did not, so there was more understanding in beasts than in a people created in the divine image and taught the law. On the ruined city three of them correct the English. Keil and Delitzsch identify the creatures as jackals; Ellicott agrees, the word meaning a howler, the mistake arising from its likeness to words rendered serpent and whale; Clarke describes the animal as an attendant on the lion that devours the refuse of his prey. Calvin adds that the threat seemed incredible to a fortified city allied with Egypt.
12:
The question is put and nobody answers it. Gill explains that what wants understanding is not the calamity but its cause, and takes the question to imply that no wise man was to be found. Wesley reads it as a challenge to search. Clarke narrows the answer: the truly wise man is the one to whom God has revealed these things, and God has revealed them to his prophet alone, so the speedy fulfilment will show he has not spoken of himself. Ellicott has sage and prophet alike called on to say why the misery is coming, asked in vain, so God answers himself through the prophet. He also tidies a loose clause, preferring and none there is that passeth through.

Calvin gets two things out of the same question. The first is astonishment, that hardly one in a hundred saw what was plain, when the prophet had spent years crying and all remained deaf. The second is encouragement, since it is the rule of wisdom to consider God's judgments before he executes them, from which it follows that the wise of this world are the foolish, hardening themselves against what stands open before their eyes. He takes the second half as a complaint that there were no prophets, then turns it into a claim: though without associate or assistant, his teaching was not on that account worth less, for God had commanded him. Henry adds the pastoral aim, to convince them they had brought this on themselves and had no cause to quarrel with God.

The answer, when God gives it, is that they forsook the law. Calvin closes the escape route in advance. They might plead that the doctrine was obscure and they went wrong for want of knowledge, but the law was set before their face; and he generalises it, that scripture is not so obscure but that anyone who can read what was revealed through Moses and the prophets is left inexcusable. On not obeying the voice he is blunter, since hypocrites do pretend to hear and nod with their ears like asses, and it is the life that must testify the voice was heard. Ellicott gives imagination its harder sense of stubbornness, and explains the plural of the false gods as a generic name covering every kind.

Calvin sets the two as opposites, there being no less contrariety between the rule of right living and men's imaginations than between fire and water, so that life cannot be rightly formed until we renounce our own devices. He reports the evasion they used, that the lesser gods were only mediators and the one God still allowed, and notes the plea was never admitted, God imputing idolatry regardless; he turns the same argument against praying to saints in his own church. The clause about the fathers draws a second application, that it is foolish to glory in imitating them as though examples stood for laws, and that a long inherited obstinacy doubles the crime rather than excusing it. Gill keeps to what the heart devised and was best pleased with.

The sentence is served as food and drink, and the first word is disputed. Ellicott identifies the plant as probably a species of Artemisia, four of which grow in the country, and observes that elsewhere it stands for moral evil, here for the bitterness of calamity. Calvin will not have the plant at all, since it is a wholesome herb and the word is never used in a good sense, and prefers bitterness. Clarke says they shall have poison instead of meat and drink. Calvin adds the sting: bread and water are the standing testimonies of paternal kindness, since we cannot eat a crumb without his goodness shining on us, and these are what get turned to poison. Wesley alone qualifies the consuming, since a full end was not in fact made.
17:
The mourning women were a trade, and Clarke describes it fully. They were paid to bewail the dead, a custom he says still obtains in Asiatic countries and in Ireland, where he has often witnessed it and supposes it came from the east. Women were used because the tender passions predominate in them, and the wailing was sung to the pipe. Ellicott adds that wailing was reduced to an art, which is why the second class of women are called cunning, and makes the sharpest observation on the summons: they are called to the funeral not of a friend or neighbour but of the nation.

Whether the prophet approves what he borrows is a real question. Calvin says plainly that he does not. The hiring of mourners is an absurd and foolish custom of almost every age, in which heirs bought feigned piety and paid women to praise the dead; scripture, he notes, often takes its similes from the vices of men, as from filth and dirt, and no one should read an endorsement into the figure. Wesley agrees, a foolish custom obtaining in most ages and countries, with tearing of hair and beating of breasts. Gill and Ellicott stay descriptive. Calvin defends the language too: the words are hyperbolical, but do not exceed the intenseness of the vengeance coming, and he was driven to them by being heard with dry eyes.

Ellicott notices what happens to the figure once applied to a whole people, an inevitable blending of metaphors, since the mourners wail for the dead nation and yet share in the obsequies themselves. Gill sees the same in the prophet putting himself among the sufferers. On the cry from the city Ellicott corrects the English again: we have left rather than we have forsaken, the received wording suggesting a voluntary abandonment the Hebrew does not carry. Keil and Delitzsch agree, glossing it as forced to leave, and reject two proposals: that the voice out of Zion belongs to Israelites already carried away, and that the dwellings are themselves the subject casting the people out, a figure too unnatural for the style here.

Teaching the daughters to wail is read as a forecast of duration or of scale. Clarke takes it as duration: not a common dirge lasting until the body is buried, but one handed on through every generation until the captivity is turned. Ellicott takes it as scale, supposing demand for mourners would outrun supply so supernumeraries had to be trained, and hears a parallel in the words spoken later to the daughters of Jerusalem. Calvin reads the shift from hired women to women at large as decisive: the calamity would touch every heart, hired lamentation would not suffice, and mercenary wailing would not be real. Gill supplies a grimmer reason for addressing women, that so many men had been killed.

What comes up at the windows is disputed. Ellicott makes it the pestilence, creeping in with its fatal taint while the invader is still held off, and corrects the last word to something nearer a market square than our street. Gill and Wesley make it the assault itself, the enemy scaling walls and breaking in at the tops of houses, with no respect to sex or age. Keil and Delitzsch keep death personified and locate the point in its suddenness, entering like a thief at night rather than because the doors are barred. Clarke has him scale the wall, take the children at play and the young men in the fields, then enter the houses for the aged and the palaces for the princes. Calvin hears derision of men who thought closed doors could shut out God. On the last verse Clarke and Ellicott both explain the reaping: the reaper drops what fills his hand for binders to gather, and here nobody gathers, so the bodies lie strewn as dung on the field.
23:
Calvin opens with a complaint about how this famous saying is handled. Many treat it as abruptly introduced, confining themselves to the words alone and so diminishing its force. He insists it looks back: the people were so swollen with confidence in their prudence, defences and wealth that the word of God counted for nothing, and the sentence is aimed at that, since all three would vanish like smoke. Ellicott reads the placement the same way, the climax of a long prophecy and the conclusion of the whole matter, that the one way of safety is to renounce reliance on the world's wisdom and wealth. He identifies the wise man as the scribe, the recognised teacher of the people.

Henry makes the three supports concrete and corporate. A man's wisdom may fail him when he needs it most; the battle is not always to the strong, since a stripling proved too hard for a giant; and riches, far from sheltering a man, may expose him and make him the fairer mark. Then he turns it on the nation: let them not boast of the wise and mighty and rich among them, as if they could hold out against the Chaldeans with wise men to advise the war, mighty men to fight it and rich men to bear its charges. Clarke reduces it to the root, that God is the fountain of all good, so riches cannot deliver in the day of death and wisdom used as a shield against him is foolishness.

Gill divides the wisdom that is forbidden into three. There is natural wisdom, often only an appearance of it and science falsely so called. There are the gifts that fit a man for public usefulness, received from above, serving others more than himself, which may fade and may be held by one who is lost at last. And there is a speculative knowledge of gospel truths, of which he says that if it is attended with conceit it is little the man knows, and if he is proud of it his knowledge is not sanctified. Calvin notes that the wise are called wise only by concession, according to common opinion, since the fear of God is the beginning of wisdom; and reports a paraphrase filling the three clauses with three named men.

What is left to glory in is knowledge of God, and Calvin explains why two words are used where one would do. They mean the same thing, but not without design: because men despised this knowledge, they had to be told that to know God is the chief part of perfect wisdom. He then turns it on his own age, where hardly one in a hundred will spend half an hour a day on it. Wesley declines to press the distinction between understanding God speculatively and knowing him practically, since both centre in this, that we so know him as to depend on him alone in every condition. Henry asks more than right apprehensions, requiring that the impressions be retained. Keil and Delitzsch put it in a sentence, that well-being comes not from reliance on one's own wisdom and strength.

The three attributes God delights in are then parcelled out. Wesley assigns each its object: kindness as it relates to his own people, judgment in punishing the wicked, righteousness in dealing justly with both. Henry hears a God not only just to all his creatures but kind to his children. Ellicott traces the verse into the apostle's hands, where it taught him what the wisdom the Corinthians prided themselves on was worth, and finds a parallel in the saying that eternal life is to know God. Clarke supplies a heathen parallel, quoting a Greek poet who told his readers not to boast of wisdom or strength or wealth, since one God alone is wise and mighty and rich indeed.
25:
The last oracle turns on a phrase the English does not carry, and Ellicott says so: better to read it as punishing all who are circumcised in uncircumcision, all who have the outward sign without the inward purity it symbolised. Calvin lays out the alternatives. The two words may be distinct, so that God visits circumcised Jews and uncircumcised nations alike; or joint, so that the threat falls on those circumcised who yet retained their uncircumcision; and he proposes a third, that the mixture had so corrupted the rite as to make it indistinguishable from heathen uncircumcision, the visitation falling on all without difference. Clarke keeps the moral even: they are not to imagine themselves the only objects of displeasure, transgressions being alike once advantages and disadvantages are fairly compared.

Why these particular nations appear together is variously explained. Clarke observes that all were delivered into the hands of the same conqueror, having generally been confederate against him. Calvin builds on the same fact: the Jews ran to Egypt whenever danger rose from the east, and the neighbouring peoples, hostile at one time and friendly at another, helped willingly once they saw their own plunder coming, so the prophet gathers into one body the allies the Jews counted on. Ellicott notices what the list does to the rite itself, since all these nations practised it, and finds scornful humour in the grouping: how could Israel pride itself on what it held in common with the nations it most abhorred. Gill adds only that these were the countries among which the Jews were dispersed.

The last group named is described by a phrase nobody agrees on. Calvin takes the words for extremity and corner literally, meaning the farthest recesses, and reads the clause as denying any hiding place: men in remote places think themselves safer for it, and he derides the confidence, since vengeance will reach the corners where they suppose they dwell safely. Clarke reports the competing readings, the ancient versions and the English margin making it those whose hair is cut short, while others thought a coastal situation meant and one the Arabians of the great desert; he prefers the margin as giving the sense of all the old versions. Ellicott is definite: they are men with the corners of their temples shorn.

He makes the epithet a nickname, comparable to round-head, given in scorn to a wild tribe who shaved the temples and let the hair grow long behind, and then draws the sting. The customs of those people were expressly forbidden to Israel, and here they stand on Israel's own level, so that if circumcision by itself secured immunity they might claim it too. On the final clause he goes further and says the English makes the prophet assert the exact opposite of what he said. It is not that these particular nations are uncircumcised, but that all the heathen are so in God's sight whether they practise the rite or not; and Israel was no better, being uncircumcised in heart.

Calvin reaches the same conclusion by his own road. In calling them uncircumcised the prophet includes the Israelites, stripping the chosen people of their distinction and making them so mingled with the nations as to be merely a part of them; the closing line resolves the contradiction, since they had the outward circumcision and not the inward. He remarks that the Idumaeans, descended from Esau, had kept the external symbol, but that their circumcision was a mockery. Then he applies it forward: the case is the same when men boast of baptism while destitute of repentance and faith, for the literal baptism avails hypocrites nothing, and one must come to the thing itself. Ellicott twice makes the prophet a forerunner of the apostle who argued that true circumcision is of the heart.
